slides.narration: Welcome to Book II, Chapter 17: Processing Data with Standard Algorithms. This deck follows the Chapter 1 Slides model: concept on the left, code or evidence on the right, and presenter notes that tell the instructor what to say and do. Modern C++ is not about using the newest syntax because it looks impressive. It is about encoding ownership, lifetime, invariants, generic behavior, and failure boundaries so the program is easier to reason about and harder to misuse.

Learners should be able to say what Processing Data with Standard Algorithms changes about program design, not merely identify a keyword. Push for three layers: the intent, the mechanism, and the evidence. In modern C++, the evidence might be a destructor running, a copy becoming independent, a move leaving ownership in exactly one place, a constrained template rejecting a bad call, or an algorithm producing a predictable sequence.

slides.title: 17.1 Searching and Sorting Collections
keyPoints: Searching and sorting algorithms answer different questions over ranges with different requirements.
Linear search needs an equality or predicate relationship.
Binary-search operations need the relevant partitioning or ordering precondition.
Sorting requires a valid ordering relation and suitable iterator capabilities.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 17, treat 17.1 Searching and Sorting Collections as a design decision with costs and evidence. Searching and sorting algorithms answer different questions over ranges with different requirements. Linear search needs an equality or predicate relationship. Binary-search operations need the relevant partitioning or ordering precondition. Sorting requires a valid ordering relation and suitable iterator capabilities. Start by writing the desired postcondition: first matching element, insertion boundary, fully ordered sequence, or stable relative order among equivalent keys. slides.title: 17.1.2 Sorting According to Custom Criteria
keyPoints: std::stable_sort preserves the original relative order of elements equivalent under the comparator.
Sorting jobs only by priority therefore retains their arrival sequence within each priority group.
Ordinary std::sort does not promise that stability.
A comparator must express a strict weak ordering for these algorithms.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 17, treat 17.1.2 Sorting According to Custom Criteria as a design decision with costs and evidence. std::stable_sort preserves the original relative order of elements equivalent under the comparator. Sorting jobs only by priority therefore retains their arrival sequence within each priority group. Ordinary std::sort does not promise that stability. A comparator must express a strict weak ordering for these algorithms. Returning true for equal elements through <= violates that contract. Avoid comparators whose answer changes during sorting because of mutable external state. When deterministic tie-breaking is required rather than original-order stability, compare a tuple of explicit keys such as priority and identifier. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.

slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 17, treat 17.2.2 Accumulating Aggregate Results as a design decision with costs and evidence. std::accumulate begins with the supplied initial value, whose type influences the accumulation. The example uses 0LL to accumulate squared integers into a long long result. Starting with integer zero and assigning the final result to a wider variable would not retroactively widen earlier intermediate accumulation. std::reduce has different grouping and ordering allowances from a simple left-to-right accumulation, especially under execution policies. Floating-point addition is not mathematically associative in finite representation, so reordered reduction can change results. Select the algorithm according to both performance and numerical reproducibility requirements rather than replacing one name with another automatically. slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 17, treat Evidence and interpretation as a design decision with costs and evidence. After stable sorting, priority-one jobs retain sequence identifiers one and three, followed by priority-two jobs zero and two. slides.title: Failure clinic — Four plausible but incorrect replacements
keyPoints: Replacing stable sorting with ordinary sorting while leaving the requirement unchanged removes a promised tie.
The sample may still pass on one library and fail on another; accidental stability is not a contract.
Replacing lower bound with a direct dereference removes the no-result branch.
Replacing back insertion with an empty vector’s begin iterator removes the destination extent.
slides.narration: In Book II, Chapter 17, treat Failure clinic — Four plausible but incorrect replacements as a design decision with costs and evidence. Replacing stable sorting with ordinary sorting while leaving the requirement unchanged removes a promised tie property. The sample may still pass on one library and fail on another; accidental stability is not a contract. Replacing lower bound with a direct dereference removes the no-result branch. Replacing back insertion with an empty vector’s begin iterator removes the destination extent. Replacing 0LL with 0 can narrow accumulation before the final assignment. These defects share a pattern: the replacement preserves the visual outline of the call while changing a hidden precondition or guarantee. Review algorithm changes with a small contract table, not only a line-by-line diff. Record range category, ordering, mutation, output extent, result lifetime, and failure behavior. The table makes semantic changes visible even when the source diff is one character. A graduate-level explanation should say what the abstraction buys, what rule keeps it honest, and what artifact proves the rule: source code, compiler acceptance or rejection, stdout, stderr, exit status, object state, or a test witness.
